title: Map & Set
description: When you need O(1) lookups, reach for `Set` (uniqueness) or `Map` (key→value).

notes: `.size` is a PROPERTY, not a method — no parens.
Map keys keep their type — m.set(1, "a") differs from m.set("1", "a"); Object keys are stringified.
Iterate a Map with `for (const [k, v] of m) { ... }`.

questions.q: How do you get the count of a Set?

questions.explain: The constructor iterates the array and drops duplicates by SameValueZero, so the two `1`s collapse into one entry — this is the whole `set-dedup` trick.

questions.q: Map vs plain Object — which is true?
options: Map keys can be any type
questions.explain: All three hold. The one that actually bites is key typing — `m.set(1, 'a')` and `m.set('1', 'a')` are two entries, where an object would stringify both to `"1"`; and an object has no `.size`, you need `Object.keys(o).length`.

questions.q: How do you check whether key `k` exists in a Map?
questions.explain: Map keys aren’t accessible via bracket notation — use .has().

exercises.prompt: Use a Set to detect the first duplicate.
Count word frequency with a Map.

L3.prompt: Write `dedupe(arr)` returning elements in original order with duplicates removed. Log `dedupe([3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,5,3])`.
hints: Track seen values in a Set.
Push to output only when not yet seen.
